title: Carrying a koan
hookLine: Rinzai students hold a koan all day and bring it to the teacher in private
last: ONE HAND — LISTEN FOR WHAT'S UNDER THE NOISE.

lines: A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.
cards: A song gets stuck in your head. Nobody decides to keep it. It just rides along: in the shower, on the drive, while you answer email, humming underneath everything else.
Koan practice does that on purpose, not with a song but with a question like mu or the sound of one hand, carried through breakfast, work and the walk home. For two weeks you've been reading koans.
But that isn't how people practice with them. It isn't done in an armchair.

teach.b: In Rinzai Zen, a student doesn't pick a koan off a shelf. The teacher gives it, usually mu or the sound of one hand to begin. Then the student carries it.
In sitting meditation, the koan is the whole practice: not thinking about it, but becoming absorbed in it, breath after breath.

teach.h: OFF THE CUSHION, INTO THE DAY.
teach.b: And, the part that surprises people, it doesn't stay on the cushion. It goes to the kitchen, the garden, the walk between buildings.
Hakuin, from yesterday, taught that practice in the middle of activity is far stronger than practice in stillness.
Korean Seon teachers say the same about the hwadu: hold it while walking, standing, sitting and lying down.
Several times a day during a retreat, and regularly the rest of the year, the student goes alone to the teacher's room. This private meeting is called dokusan, or sanzen.
The student bows and presents the koan, not with an explanation but with a response: sometimes a word, a gesture, a silence.
Often the teacher rings a small hand bell and the meeting is over. Not yet; go back and keep going. Some students hear that bell for months.
By custom, what happens in the room stays in the room; students don't share their answers.
That's one reason the published books of answers miss the point: a response only counts if it comes from you, in the moment, face to face. Passing the first koan doesn't end the work.
Many more follow, each opening the first seeing a little wider.

how: Rinzai Zen students receive a koan from their teacher, hold it in sitting and daily work, and present their response in private interviews called dokusan or sanzen, several times a day during retreats.

games.q: you're in the teacher's room with mu. you've read a book that lists the 'right answer'. what happens if you give it?
o: the teacher passes you at once.
the teacher probably rings the bell: not yet.
the teacher asks which book it was.
games.why: a response only counts if it comes from you, face to face; borrowed answers usually meet the bell.

practice: Bring back mu, the first koan, and let it ride the out-breath the way you did eleven days ago: not thinking about it, just the sound, all the way out.
Then imagine standing up and carrying it into one chore, the dishes, folding clothes, the walk to the mailbox, mu with each step, each plate.

wordCard.voice: Dokusan. The private meeting where a Zen student brings a response to the koan to the teacher alone.

orig.note: Japanese dokusan: going alone (to the teacher), the private koan interview.

carryVoice: Your line: carry it. On the cushion, and off it, all day long. Day two hundred eighty-nine.
